A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GESPI research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations and experiments involving protein structure prediction, LLM comparisons, outlier detection, and vision-transformer interpretability.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical studies and adds classification experiments, majority-vote comparisons, and further controlled analyses.

M1.justification: The main GESPI aggregation and base algorithms remain unchanged. However, Appendix H.1 changes the prescribed tolerance from ε = rδ/(n+1) − α to ε = 1 − α − rδ/(n+1), altering the stated tuning rule for that conformal specialization. This does not establish a change to the experimental implementation.

E1.justification: V2 adds class-conditional image classification using 30 ImageNet classes and corresponding FLUX images. This extends the represented classes and introduces prediction-set evaluation beyond v1's animal/non-animal interpretability task using ImageNet. The earlier application coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds the evaluated Guardrail comparator across applications and simulations, Synth+Real comparisons in Appendix J, and a direct SPI comparison in Figure S10. V1 described guardrail and pooling components but did not report these as separate comparators; SPI was discussed without an empirical comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include classification with 15 real, 1,000 synthetic, and 500 test images per class; comparisons at matched empirical coverage or FWER; and DeepSeek-7B majority-vote configurations K = 1, 4, 8, 16, 64. The protein risk levels and both outlier trimming proportions already appeared in v1, despite their changed placement.

E4.justification: V2 adds matched-coverage variance analyses for both guardrail variants, sensitivity to synthetic sample size against SPI, and empirical power-versus-FWER analyses under different synthetic-data qualities. Figures S6–S10 and S18 examine questions beyond the retained simulation sweeps and trimming experiments.

E5.justification: Tables S3–S4 introduce explicit standard-error reporting, and Appendix B.1 specifies 100 different data splits for classification. V1 already reported repeated trials and standard deviations for the interpretability study. Stated repetition counts for retained experiments remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Substantial results are added. Tables S3–S4 report Magpie coverage of 95.8% and mean set size 4.0 for GESPI, versus 100% and 30 for OnlyReal. Figure S14 adds majority-vote findings, including little evidence favoring K = 64 over 16. Guardrail, Synth+Real, SPI, and matched-error results further expand the evidence.

T1.justification: Localized mathematical corrections include composite one-sided nulls and their binomial-test justification, the meet condition in F.1, changing > k to ≥ k in Appendix G's k-FWER definition, the ε formula in H.1, and replacing TV with KL inside the Pinsker bound in I.7. The principal theoretical framework and proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The general wrapper and distribution-free guardrail contributions remain. Section 1.1 newly foregrounds variance reduction and ROC improvements as principal benefits. It also qualifies v1's assertion of tight α control with good synthetic data to saying that the error rate can approach α as quality improves.

C2.justification: V2 explains variance reduction at matched coverage, distinguishes visual realism from statistical usefulness, and qualifies matched-error comparisons as illustrative. It discusses the loss of ROC advantage at 5% trimming. Appendix J additionally makes an overly broad claim of pooled-data and synthetic-only similarity, which Figure S30 does not uniformly support.

D1.justification: New documentation identifies CLIP with APS for classification, SPI's β = 0.4, and majority-vote configurations. The existing permutation test's one-sided direction is clarified. The Credit Card reference loses its dataset URL, while the code link continues to identify the same repository.

R1.justification: V2 sharpens the contrast with SPI through pooling, sample-efficiency, and flexibility comparisons, and adds Romano et al. (2020) for APS. Prediction-powered inference discussion largely moves to Appendix A. FLUX's renamed author attribution and SPI's publication update refer to existing works.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around practical choices, validity, utility, and the tolerance tradeoff. The main experiments are reorganized around classification, proteins, and multiple outlier testing; LLM comparisons move to Appendix C. Related-work organization and the experimental appendices are also restructured.

P2.justification: V2 adds classification plots, matched-error curves, majority-vote displays, and per-class tables. Existing plots gain comparator series and revised legends; protein panels are regrouped, and the main outlier figure incorporates an ROC display. Appendix J redisplays many experiments with Synth+Real. The protein visualizations are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical case beyond comparisons against a more conservative real-only procedure. Added Guardrail comparisons and matched-error analyses in Figure 5 and Figures S7–S8 and S18 help distinguish synthetic-data benefits from simply relaxing error tolerance, while exposing a setting with little power advantage. New classification evidence, standard errors, and mathematical corrections further improve the paper. These gains outweigh Appendix J's overbroad claim that pooled and synthetic-only baselines consistently perform similarly.
